clauses: The King had just returned from hunting, and the glare of the sun had so dazzled his eyes that he found it difficult to read the petition brought to him.
There was a page waiting in the hall, and upon him the King called.
He did not articulate distinctly, but huddled his words together as if they were one long word.
"Stop!" said the King, impatiently, and sent for the page's companion.
Another page entered, and to him the King gave the petition.
The King jokingly asked him whether he had not slept in the public garden with the gate open.
He determined that he would avoid the mistake which his comrade had made, and commenced reading the petition slowly.
But his manner was so tedious that the King cried out, "Stop! are you reciting a lesson?"
The girl pointed out by the King was a daughter of one of the laborers, and had come to help her father weed the flower beds.
Now, Ernestine was fond of reading aloud, and often the neighbors would assemble at her father's house to hear her.
The King gave her the petition, and she rapidly glanced through the opening lines to get some idea of what it was about.
Ernestine read it with so much feeling that when she had finished, the King exclaimed that he now understood, and dismissed the two pages from his service for one year.
note: Three male entities (King, first page, second page) co-present in a court scene; clause 2 'He did not articulate' is same-gender ambiguous between the King (agent one clause earlier) and the first page (just introduced as recipient), resolving to the page; clause 6 'He determined' is the same trap for the second page. Ernestine (female) is introduced separately and provides the pronoun->name-linking contrast entity.
verification: Excerpted/paraphrased from a long story (g5 clean lines 1-25); clauses 0-11 compress ~10 source paragraphs so some connective material was dropped -- director should confirm the paraphrase in clauses 6-7 (the second page's self-conceit and tedious reading) preserves the original causal chain. Unsure whether 'first_page'/'second_page' should instead be surfaced to the reader as literally unnamed (no proper name ever given in source), which may make this a harder distractor case than the fully-named passages already in gold_multientity_dense_v1.

clauses: "A stranger, mother," said the man who answered the door; "and he wants us to let him stay all night."
The woman looked at the stranger doubtingly, and said, "We don't keep a public house."
"Too far for a tired man to go on foot," said the master of the house, kindly; "we must give him a bed."
The girl had drawn quietly to her mother's side, and one small fair hand rested on the woman's hand.
The woman's repulsive aspect changed into one of kindly welcome, and she said she guessed they could find a place for him.
"Dick!" said the farmer, giving the rein a quick jerk, but Dick moved not a step.
A stout lad now came out into the road, and, catching Dick by the bridle, jerked him forward.
But Dick met this new ally with increased stubbornness, planting his fore feet more firmly.
The impatient boy now struck the pony on the side of the head with his clinched hand, and jerked cruelly at his bridle.
"Don't do so, John!" the maiden's voice reached the narrator's ear; she had taken hold of the lad and drawn him away from the animal, and he obeyed her wish.
"Poor Dick!" said the maiden, as she stroked his neck lightly.
The pony turned toward her, and rubbed his head against her arm; then he started off at a light, cheerful trot.
"What a wonderful power that hand possesses!" said the narrator to his companion; he looked at the narrator for a moment, then said, "She's good! Everybody and everything loves her."
note: Farmer, John (lad), and Dick (male pony) are ALL referred to with he/him/his, a cross-species same-gender trap layered on top of a human same-gender pair (farmer vs John); clause 9 'he obeyed her wish' resolves to John (the lad just pulled away), not Dick or the farmer, and is the sharpest trap since John and Dick were both patients in the immediately preceding clauses.
verification: Excerpted from 'Gentle Hand' (g5 clean lines 51-101); the first-person narrator ('I') was dropped/converted to 'the narrator' to keep the entity set to co-present story characters -- director should decide whether the narrator itself should be a tracked entity (assumed male by convention of the era's first-person travel-sketch narrators, not explicitly stated in this excerpt). Also unsure whether clause 3's 'the girl' before her name is ever given (she is called 'the maiden' / 'Gentle Hand' throughout the source, never a proper name) counts as a fair same-entity link or should be flagged as a harder no-proper-name case.

clauses: The barber overheard a minister's text on keeping the Sabbath holy, and became convinced that he was breaking the law by shaving customers on the Lord's day.
The barber took courage and opened his mind to his minister, who advised him to give up Sabbath work.
The barber discontinued his Sabbath work and went constantly to public worship; his genteel customers left him, and he was nicknamed "Puritan."
He was obliged to give up his fashionable shop and take a cellar under the old market house.
A stranger from one of the coaches asked for a barber, and was directed by the hostler to the cellar.
The stranger requested to be shaved quickly, as he did not like to violate the Sabbath.
The barber burst into tears, and asked the stranger to lend him a half-penny to buy a candle.
When shaved, the stranger asked the barber his name, and the barber answered, "William Reed."
"Come along, follow me," said the stranger; "your uncle is dead, and has left an immense fortune, which I will put you in possession of."
The stranger, who was a pious attorney, told the barber that he had advertised him in vain, and had great pleasure in transferring the fortune to the rightful heir.
note: Only two entities, both male, but a very dense two-way pronoun chain across 10 clauses with alternating agent/recipient roles (barber then stranger then barber again); clause 5's 'he did not like to violate the Sabbath' is same-gender ambiguous between the stranger (subject of the sentence) and the barber (topic of the immediately preceding three clauses about Sabbath observance), and resolves to the stranger -- a topic-vs-subject-continuity trap.
verification: Excerpted from g5 clean lines 269-281. Only 2 entities co-present (below the 3+ density bar used for most existing gold_multientity_dense_v1 records) -- included anyway because the PRONOUN CHAIN density and topic/subject-continuity trap are unusually strong even with just 2 referents; director should judge whether 2-entity passages belong in this file or should be a separate weaker-density control tier.

clauses: The Duke, by well applied argument and personal application, gained a single decisive vote, and the gentleman he recommended won the election.
In gratitude, the Duke poured forth promises on the voter, calling him his best and dearest friend, and said he would serve him by night or by day.
The voter thanked the Duke for his kindness, and told him the supervisor of excise was old and infirm, asking him to recommend his relative for the post.
"My dear friend, why do you ask for such a trifling employment?" exclaimed the Duke; "your relative shall have it the moment the place is vacant."
"The instant the man dies," replied the Duke, "set out posthaste for London, and thunder at my door; I will leave word with my porter to show you upstairs directly."
The parties separated; the Duke drove to a friend's house, without a wish to see his new acquaintance again, but the voter remembered the promise well.
The supervisor died a few months after, and the voter, relying on the Duke's word, traveled to London posthaste and ascended the steps of the Duke's palace.
The Duke had sat up anxiously expecting dispatches, and, wearied, retired to rest, having instructed his porter not to go to bed, as he expected a messenger with important news.
The porter, settled for the night in his armchair, had already begun a nap, when the vigorous arm of the voter roused him from his slumbers.
To the voter's question, "Is the Duke at home?" the porter replied, "Yes, and in bed; but he has left particular orders that, come when you will, you are to go up to him directly."
"Is he dead?" exclaimed the Duke, rubbing his eyes, scarcely awakened.
"Yes, my lord," replied the voter, delighted to find the election promise still fresh in the Duke's memory.
note: Three male entities (Duke, Cornish voter, porter) co-present at the climax; clause 9 stacks 'he has left orders...you are to go up to him' where both 'he' and 'him' are the Duke, spoken by the porter (a third party) to the voter (the addressee) -- the pronoun refers OUTSIDE the current speaker/addressee dyad, the same class of trap as the Joab/Absalom passage already in gold_multientity_dense_v1 but from an unrelated comic-anecdote story, useful as a second independent instance of that construction.
verification: Excerpted/paraphrased from g6 clean lines 1-33 (a long anecdote); clauses 0-11 compress roughly 15 source paragraphs including dialogue given as unattributed quoted turns in the source -- director should double check clause 4 and clause 10's quoted dialogue attributions (Duke vs voter vs porter) against the raw source since several turns in the middle of the anecdote were dropped for length and the remaining turns were re-stitched.

clauses: Chub had long been urging Frank Meriwether to make additions to his collection of literature, and Frank gave way to the argument, partly to gratify the parson.
The matter was committed to Chub, who set out on a voyage of exploration, and contrived to execute his commission with curious felicity.
After the books arrived, Chub spent a whole week arranging the volumes on their shelves, having altered the arrangement at least seven times.
After this, Chub regularly spent his evenings in the library, and Frank was hardly behind the parson in this fancy.
Ned had seldom joined the two in their philosophical retirement; it was whispered that Chub was giving Frank a quiet course of lectures in ancient philosophy.
One dreary winter night, Ned, having waited for the philosophers until midnight, set out to invade their retreat, not doubting he should find them deep in study.
When Ned entered the library, the parson was discovered asleep over a book, while Frank, in another chair, was snoring over a folio.
Frank started up in great consternation upon hearing Ned's footstep beside him, and, from that time, almost entirely deserted the library.
Chub, however, was not so easily drawn away, and still shows his hankering after his leather-coated friends.
note: Three male entities (Chub, Frank, Ned) co-present; clause 7 'hearing Ned's footstep beside him' has 'him' same-gender ambiguous between Frank (agent of 'started up', most locally salient) and Chub (also present, asleep in the same room per clause 6) -- resolves to Frank via the surrounding predicate ('started up... deserted the library' is consistently about Frank), a same-clause pronoun-stacking trap among 3 co-present males.
verification: Excerpted/paraphrased from g6 clean lines 789-805 ('Swallow Barn'). Note the source text uses 'Hazard' once as an apparent alternate name/nickname for Ned ('a discovery made by Hazard' then 'Ned had seldom joined...') -- I treated Hazard and Ned as the SAME referent based on context, but this is an inference, not explicit in the excerpt; director should verify against the fuller original text before trusting this identity link, since a same-noun-different-referent or nickname-confusion error here would be exactly the kind of mistake this file is meant to avoid propagating.
